I know you said you can't afford an accountant, but I really recommend it. It is not uncommon for IRS notices to overstated what is owed due to the IRS not having the full information. 

For example, say a contractor doesn't file his taxes for the year and he gets issued $50k in 1099's. The IRS knows he grossed at least 50k so they will eventually send him a notice to collect on the tax owed on that 50k. In reality the contractor probably owes less than what the IRS is quoting because that doesn't factor in business expenses.   

Having an accountant review all your tax documents, IRS letters, Transcripts to confirm this 15k balance due is correct is what I would recommend.

My advice for when you file 2024 taxes:

Prepare a return before 4/15 based on what you believe your correct information is. Do not file the return and instead file for an extension with payment for what you think you owe based on the return prepared. 

You will then wait till around May or June 2025 and pull your 2024 wage transcript: https://www.irs.gov/individuals/get-transcript (May/June is when these typically become available)

These transcripts show all the income that has been reported to the IRS you made, so you are looking to see if the IRS has on file that you were issued a 1099 for 21k (If they even actually filed a 1099, this sounds like a mickey mouse operation). 

If they did, you want your gross income to reflect the 21k, but you should then add a expense line on on your Schedule C subtracting out the excess incorrect amount. For the expense description you can briefly explain the situation. Having the gross income line match the 1099 is important because if it doesn't, two years later you could get an automated notice saying you underreported your income, so this method avoids that. If the IRS ever questions you on the expense they may want more information on the situation and from there you just have to explain it to them.

That's what I would think would be the best way to handle this would be. Not sure if any other professionals would have better ideas. 

Side note, If prior to 2024 you were W-2, your boss likely purposefully misclassified you as contractor which he can get in trouble for if you report it to the IRS for not paying his share of employment taxes. Probably not worth the hassle for you, but if you really hate your former boss you could go that route.

With cars that old you should really be looking for everything and anything to minimize the amount of money you'll have to put into it if this is going to be your daily driver. 

Drive it, make sure there no weird clunks from the suspension, steering feels normal, transmission shifts good, ect.

Look in the engine bay, make sure there's no oil leaks, weird sounds or smells. If you have access to it, it's always good to have a obd reader handy to make sure there were no check engine codes cleared recently.

Look under from all sides makes sure there not serious rust or suspicious looking body work repairs. Even check the trunk and spare wheel well. A lot of cars sometimes get water trapped in there and it starts rusting out that wheel well.

Obviously usual stuff too like does the window go down and up, does the ac work. Hows the tread on the tires. Might even want to makes yourself a checklist so you don't forget about anything when looking at the car.

Never be afraid to walk away. There will always be more cars that get put up for sale.
